summary:
The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus, including Stavropol Krai, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. The note finds that trans people and people who publicly advocate for LGBT+ rights in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

The same note records systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people across the North Caucasus between 2017 and 2024, and states that the 2023 extremist designation attracts two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising.

Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to Russia and names the Stavropol region among areas subject to frequent terrorist attacks. The same advisory reports that 2SLGBTQI+ persons and the families of their allies have been attacked, harassed and abused, that advocacy organisations have been treated as extremist since January 2024, and it warns that foreign visitors are placed under surveillance.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, a regional defender speaking in exile to the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He reports year-on-year deterioration across the region; the most recent documented period of systematic regional campaigns in this record ends in 2024, and no later instance is documented.
tangentialFactors:
Global Affairs Canada requires Ministry of Interior special permission for entry to Kabardino-Balkaria including Elbrus, Karachai-Cherkessia and North Ossetia, neighbouring North Caucasus territories; Stavropol Krai itself is not listed among the permission-required areas.

The UK Home Office assessment of Russia outside the North Caucasus is non-persecutory, so the risk level described here is specific to this region rather than a restatement of the national picture.

The Canadian advisory's warning that foreign visitors are under surveillance applies to Russia generally and is not limited to this region.
localsOnly:
Residents of the North Caucasus face systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people documented between 2017 and 2024, with public advocacy of LGBT+ rights treated as extremist and carrying two to six years' imprisonment, or six to ten years for organising.

Private existence carries risk for local LGBTIQ+ people: David Isteev reports that even discreet life can lead to violence, detention or forced return to families, and describes deterioration year on year.

Advocacy organisations have been treated as extremist since January 2024, removing lawful channels through which residents might seek protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Stavropol Krai-specific incident, prosecution or killing with a date is documented in this inventory; the regional findings rest on country-level advisories that name the region and on a regional defender's testimony, neither of which supplies case-level detail for the krai.

Whether Stavropol Krai has recorded its own extremism convictions under the 2023 designation is not sourced here, and no regional enforcement statistics are available in the inventory.

The terrorist-attack frequency cited for the Stavropol region carries no figures or period in the source, so its magnitude cannot be assessed.
